propositions.text: Section F of the Refugee Convention lists crimes that exclude persons from protection, requiring serious reasons for consideration.
propositions.quote: Section F of article 1 of the Convention is relevant. It reads as follows: F. The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (a) he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crimes; (b) he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee; (c) he has been guilty of acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

propositions.text: The Minister must prove the male claimant falls within the exclusion criteria; direct crimes against humanity are not claimed.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the Minister to prove that the male claimant falls within the category of excluded persons. Counsel for the Minister did not claim that the male claimant himself had directly committed crimes against humanity.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister bears the burden to prove exclusion; direct crimes are not claimed against the claimant.

propositions.text: Principles from case law define the level of participation needed to establish complicity in international crimes.
propositions.quote: De Montigny J., in Pineda Collins v. M.C.I., summarizes the principles previously established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Ramirez, Moreno and Sivakumar.

paragraphs.summary: Case law outlines the participation level required for complicity in crimes.

propositions.text: The male claimant was a member of the Burundian army from 1973 to 1993, during which the army was dominated by Tutsis and committed serious human rights violations.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was a member of the Burundian army for 20 years, from 1973 to 1993. Numerous documents entered on the record show the army's complete domination by the Tutsi ethnic group during that period (and before) and the extremely serious human rights violations of which the army was guilty.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant served in a Tutsi-dominated army involved in serious violations.

propositions.text: Pre-1973 events, including ethnic violence and massacres, are summarized by a report from 1995, not attributable to the claimant.
propositions.quote: The introduction reads as follows: In the particular Burundian context, a short comment on the concept of minority/majority is called for.

paragraphs.summary: Pre-1973 ethnic violence is summarized in a 1995 report, not attributable to the claimant.

propositions.text: In 1965, a failed coup led to the killing of the Hutu political elite, ending their political involvement for years.
propositions.quote: In 1965, a failed coup was violently repressed. The entire Hutu political elite was killed, which ended all Hutu political involvement for many years.

paragraphs.summary: 1965 coup repression resulted in the killing of Hutu leaders, ending their political role.

propositions.text: The 1972 attempted coup was followed by massacres of Hutus, with hundreds of thousands killed and many exiled.
propositions.quote: In 1972, another attempted coup was followed by the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus and the exile of another 300,000.

paragraphs.summary: The 1972 coup attempt led to mass killings and exile of Hutus.

propositions.text: Military regimes from 1976 to 1987, dominated by Tutsis, continued discrimination and repression of Hutus.
propositions.quote: From 1976, Colonel Bagaza overthrew the regime, and the army remained a major force. The army was Tutsi-dominated, and Hutus faced discrimination.

paragraphs.summary: Tutsi-dominated military regimes from 1976 to 1987 continued Hutu repression.

propositions.text: The 1972 massacre of Hutus is corroborated by many documents in the record.
propositions.quote: The preceding events, specifically, of course, the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus in 1972, are corroborated by many of the documents entered on the record.

paragraphs.summary: The 1972 Hutu massacre is supported by multiple documents.

propositions.text: In 1988, the army was almost entirely Tutsi, and massacres of Hutus occurred, with many fleeing to Rwanda.
propositions.quote: In 1988, the Burundian army was almost entirely made up of Tutsis... Hutu gangs massacred hundreds of Tutsis, and many Hutus fled to Rwanda.

paragraphs.summary: The 1988 Tutsi army and Hutu massacres led to many Hutu refugees in Rwanda.

propositions.text: Reyntjens describes the 1988 military repression as a massacre targeting Hutus, with estimates of 20,000 killed and many refugees.
propositions.quote: Reyntjens described the situation as a massacre by the Burundian army, with estimates of 20,000 killed and 60,000 Hutus fleeing to Rwanda.

paragraphs.summary: The 1988 repression was a massacre of Hutus, with thousands killed and refugees fleeing to Rwanda.

propositions.text: The facts relating to the 1988 massacre are reported in other documents entered on the record.
propositions.quote: The facts relating to this massacre in August 1988 are reported in other documents entered on the record.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 61 states that facts about the 1988 massacre are documented in other record documents.

propositions.text: Buyoya implemented changes to integrate Hutus into public institutions, which was resisted by the army.
propositions.quote: Pressured by the international community, Buyoya implemented significant changes and began to integrate Hutus into public institutions. However, the army resisted the change.

propositions.text: In November 1991, Hutu militants attacked a police station and a military post, leading to many deaths.
propositions.quote: On November 23, 1991, poorly armed Hutu militants attacked a police station in XXXX and a military post in the province of Cibitoke. The army's retaliation caused the deaths of more than 1,000 people, according to the various reports. The government admitted that 500 people died.

propositions.text: International human rights monitors confirm the army committed crimes against humanity over years.
propositions.quote: This documentary evidence leaves no doubt that the Burundian army committed, over numerous years, crimes against humanity. This evidence comes from key international human rights monitors and is not contradicted. The panel finds it to be credible and trustworthy.

propositions.text: Crime against humanity involves four elements: proscribed act, attack, civilian target, and knowledge of attack.
propositions.quote: Mugesera v. Canada36 defines crime against humanity as follows: 119 As we shall see, based on the provisions of the Criminal Code and the principles of international law, a criminal act rises to the level of a crime against humanity when four elements are made out: 1. An enumerated proscribed act was committed (this involves showing that the accused committed the criminal act and had the requisite guilty state of mind for the underlying act); 2. The act was committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack; 3. The attack was directed against any civilian population or any identifiable group of persons; and 4. The person committing the proscribed act knew of the attack and knew or took the risk that his or her act comprised a part of that attack.

propositions.text: Murder is a proscribed act; attack on thousands is systematic; attack was against Hutu civilians; army knew of the attack.
propositions.quote: Murder is clearly a proscribed act and meets the first criterion. When the victims are in the thousands, it must be concluded that the attack is necessarily a systematic attack at the least. The second criterion is therefore met. The third criterion requires that the attack be directed against a civilian population or an identified group; the documentary evidence shows that the Hutu civilian population was the victim of attacks by the army for years. Finally, the person, that is, the Burundian army, was aware of the context of the attack. That also goes without saying.

propositions.text: The panel concludes the army committed crimes against humanity in 1965, 1972, 1988, and 1991.
propositions.quote: The panel therefore concludes that in 1965, 1972, 1988 and 1991, the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity against the Hutu civilian population.

propositions.text: The Minister did not allege the army was directed toward a limited purpose.
propositions.quote: However, the Minister did not allele that the Burundian army was an organization directed toward a limited and brutal purpose. In fact, it certainly had other functions.

propositions.text: The Minister did not allege the male claimant participated in massacres, only that he was complicit by association.
propositions.quote: The Minister also did not allege that the male claimant had participated personally in any massacres. Rather, he alleged that it was as a member of the army that he was complicit in crimes against humanity committed by the Burundian army. Therefore, he was allegedly complicit by association in the crimes.

propositions.text: The panel finds the male claimant's ignorance of the crimes not credible and concludes he was aware of the crimes.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that this statement is not credible. First, it is contradicted in his own PIF and in XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006. ... It is impossible that the male claimant did not know this fact at the time he joined the army.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraphs discuss the 1991 coup, the claimant's legal issues, threats, family claim, Minister's allegations, and evidence of army crimes against humanity, concluding the claimant was aware of these crimes.

propositions.text: The panel finds that the male claimant did not try to dissociate himself from the army and could have left before 1993.
propositions.quote: he did not try to dissociate himself. The panel is of the opinion that these problems did not affect his safety and could not be a valid reason for the male claimant to maintain his association with the army.

propositions.text: Whether the male claimant's association with the army affects his safety and eligibility for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The panel discusses the male claimant's lack of dissociation from the army and his ability to leave before 1993, affecting his safety considerations.

propositions.text: The male claimant held a leadership position within the army and had 'guilty knowledge' of crimes, making him more morally responsible.
propositions.quote: The more important the position held by a person in an organization that has committed one or more crimes, the more likely his or her complicity.

propositions.text: Leadership positions in organizations responsible for crimes increase moral responsibility and complicity.

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes that holding a leadership role and having guilty knowledge increases moral responsibility for crimes.

propositions.text: The male claimant is considered to have committed a crime against humanity and is excluded from protection under the Act.
propositions.quote: there are serious reasons for considering that the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and must be excluded from the protection that can be granted under the Act.

propositions.text: The male claimant is excluded from protection under the Act due to serious reasons of complicity in crimes against humanity.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and is excluded from protection.

propositions.text: The male claimant is a person referred to in article 1F(a) of the Convention and cannot be considered a refugee.
propositions.quote: the male claimant, XXX XXXX, is a person referred to in article 1F(a) of the Convention. Consequently, ... cannot be considered a refugee.

propositions.text: The male claimant is not considered a refugee under section 98 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the male claimant is excluded from refugee status under article 1F(a).

propositions.text: The female claimants have established a serious possibility of persecution based on membership in a particular social group.
propositions.quote: they have satisfactorily discharged their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on one of the grounds set out in the Convention.

propositions.text: The female claimants are recognized as Convention refugees under section 96 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the female claimants have established refugee status based on membership in a particular social group.
